put away.sentence: The prosecutor, speaking for the side that wants things put away, immediately demands its removal.
But the defense says, "If I put it away, I might forget to take it."
But what might change if it is put away?
For the person who wants it put away, it's "something in the way."
If you ask, "Why don't you put that away?" the conversation can turn into an interrogation.
Before putting something away, ask what it helps with.

in the way.sentence: For the person who wants it put away, it's "something in the way."

force away.sentence: If you simply order, "Straight into the cupboard!" and force it away, the kitchen will look neat.

leave out.sentence: Today's topic is The Trial of "Leaving Things Out" Is Now in Session.
A thing left out in a shared home can mean different things to different people.
Do you have any "working things left out" at home?
But don't rush to announce, "Science proves that if you leave it out, you won't forget!"
The story asks us to look at things left out with care, because they may have a purpose.

in sight.sentence: By being in sight, it helps someone remember—in a way, it's a "kitchen reminder."
So far, we've heard that keeping the supplement in sight can help someone remember to take it.
A scorecard that says "the fewer things in sight, the better" could end up taking points away from the ways each home has found to make life work.
The supplement example is the participant's own explanation; the study did not test whether keeping it in sight works.
A study of New Zealand households suggests that clutter can sometimes support daily life, as when one person kept supplements in sight to remember them.
